137.t: Mother, brothers and cousins who played music
137.s: His mother was not musical but his brothers Joe, Earl and Roosevelt and cousins Clyde and Allen all played; he sorts out the birth order and instruments.
137.q: Well, I had three, outside of myself. And the other ones was my cousins. And so everybody thought they were brothers, so they just growed up in our family, too. All their people deceased. There was Clyde and Allen and all those ones that they --

137.t: Joe's instruments, urging study and the family bands
137.s: Joe played trumpet, bass and violin and wrote music; he pushed his brothers to read, bought Eddie's trombone, and they played as the Durham Brothers and Dixie Ramblers.
137.q: I had two or three of them in a box. They come by sets, see. When (inaudible) and after he gets past ________, he adds rattlers, and that's what they take, they sound, and you take them out, and they're dead in that shoebox. But after you dry them out, zoom you can hear that sound.

34.t: Straightening out the Cato family tree
34.s: The interviewer sorts out the Catos; Pasley adds his aunts who played piano after Catholic school training.
34.q: He had a, Adam had a sister named Velma. She could play. My aunt played good music. You know, play music. My aunt Laura, she could play the piano by music. Yeah. Only by music. Yeah. They learn it in the Catholic schools. I see. Yeah. Very interesting. All of them learn it in the Catholic schools.…

255.s: His grandfather, father and uncles all played guitar and string music in a French-speaking family band.
255.q: Well, my grandfather, he played guitar. All my uncles, aunts on my father's side. My father, he played guitar. Played guitar. And I had one uncle on my mother's side. He played guitar, which was Eugene. Oh. That's my middle name. Maybe after he was a guitar player.

185.t: Uncles Marcus and Louis, father Lorenzo Sr., and brother as reed players
185.s: Tio describes his guitarist aunts, his uncles Marcus and Louis (the latter a bassoon player) and his father Lorenzo Sr., with his brother following the father on all reed instruments.
185.q: And my grandfather's sister was a guitarist. And they moved here after my grandfather died. My grandmother moved here, which I had an uncle, Marcus Teo. He was an also crying at us.

251.t: His father's violin teachers and musical relatives
251.s: Albert describes his father's violin teachers and young relatives who played and died early, and family lesson exchanges.
251.q: Yes, there were two or three men involved with him. One of them was the old man, Valtair, that I can remember vividly. And the others came from within the family. I had an uncle that was a great violin player. He died real young. Naval. They call him Naval.

267.t: Uncle's family bands and a visit from Jay McShann
267.s: Ford's uncle used the whole family on jobs, with other musician families, and music was constant at home. Jay McShann once came to the house and gave them notes to play.
267.q: My uncle was working, my Uncle Presley was working with Jay McShane's band. He came to the house, which was right across from where my Uncle Oxlade's done. One corner, another uptown, downtown. And Jay McShane, which is known as a blues pianist, and he was singing the blues, and he'd give us each a…

628.t: Musicians in the family and the Ninth Ward players
628.s: Only a guitar-playing relative of his mother's played in the family; Allen asks about Ninth Ward musicians, and Williams says they came up later than he did.
628.ch: Beginnings and early New Orleans scene
628.q: No, it wasn't. One was a, he was a guitar player. And that was Reverend Griffin's brother, Kenderman, you know, my mother. He was a guitar player. What was his name? Nah, I can't think of his name now. He did so long, man.

828.t: Father the guitarist and the forgotten violinist
828.s: His father played guitar and worked with a famous violinist whose name Lanoix cannot recall; no one else in the family played music.
828.q: Well, there's one man that he worked with, was very famous, but he was a violinist. Oh, I can't think of that man's name now. He was very famous.

776.t: Musical talents in the family and the first combination
776.s: The brothers play piano and violin; the first combination was piano, violin and drums.
776.q: And then, I was a band of drums.

877.t: A musical family; father John Handy the violinist
877.s: Whole family was musical; his father John Handy played all instruments, professionally violin, mandolin and guitar, by ear.
877.q: Well, the whole family was musical. The whole family. Mother, father, sister, brothers. All the whole family was musical. What was your father's name? What did he play? John Hand.

291.t: Brothers who played the fife in New Orleans
291.s: Barnes says his brother Mealy led the family in playing the fife, which he took up at six. Another older brother was accidentally shot trying to stop a fight.
291.q: Yes, I had one, but he didn't take up an instrument, but he used to play a fife just like I did. Oh really? Yeah. Just the same as my oldest brother, Mealy. He's the ringleader of it. He played the fife. And during those times the fife was very popular around New Orleans. If you don't know what a…

306.t: His musician father Boss and his mother who played guitar
306.s: Rene describes his father as a born string player and repairer and his mother playing guitar and singing; Slow Drag knew his father, called Boss, and Rene recalls a childhood chase. He also boasts of his triple tom-tom solo on Caravan.
306.q: Well my daddy, my daddy was, he was a born musician. He used to work for Roy Lyre years ago. I understand he was the first man to put the foil in the ghetto. That's what I understand. He played ghetto, in other words he played all string instruments. Then he could repair stringing. He could make…

637.s: He had two brothers and two sisters, including Albert Nicholas, and talks about taking up cornet and clarinet.
637.q: Well, my brother used to play in Orange County. He used to go around. He used to go around. He used to play good. Get the date. Kind of.

886.s: His father played in brass bands only, taught the sons, and died around 1931 at 54.
886.q: No, it was brass bands. Just brass bands? Yes, he taught us to play brass bands.

638.t: Family: brother John, father's harmonica and guitar, Catholic church
638.s: His older brother John is a drummer; his father played harmonica and guitar with a friend Newt; his mother only sang hymns.
638.q: Older than me. John Mosley. Mm-hmm. I'm his, I'm 50, I'm 62 and he is 64. That's a couple of years. He's two years older than me.

392.t: Uncle Joe the songwriter and family background
392.s: Uncle Joe wrote songs including the Axe Man piece; a grandfather played cello; family from Portugal and France.
392.q: Yeah, he died about, uh, he died about, uh, ten, twelve years ago. He was no, uh, uh, no versatile musician, but he'd played the piano by ear, and he could manage to put a few notes down on paper, you see. But he, uh, I guess he had written and recorded many, many songs. Uh, Gene Austin recorded…

177.t: Father-in-law, the sousaphone player, and his brass bands
177.s: His father-in-law played sousaphone in brass bands such as Gagne's.
177.q: About her father, no, because at the time that he went there she didn't know too much about music.

300.t: Little Dad, the hard-of-hearing musician in Humphrey's band
300.s: Humphrey remembers Little Dad, who was hard to talk to but never made a bad note, and his carnival-day brothers.
300.q: Well, that's where his people stay there. I seen a little fella there yesterday. Mm-hmm. I got home. Mm-hmm. He got there. Looked like it's all in their family.

707.t: Musical family: Gunsey Montgomery's band and ten siblings
707.s: His great-uncle led a band; father, mother, brothers and sisters all played.
707.q: Well, I had a uncle, great uncle, my father's uncle. He had a band. His name was Gunsey Montgomery. He had the big four band out of Norleene, Louisiana.

978.t: His wife's and family's musical background and his aunt's gift of his first instrument
978.s: His wife and her sisters were singers, relatives played various instruments, he practiced in the barbershop, and his aunt bought his first instrument.
978.q: She did? It did. A good deal to help me and improvise. Uh-huh. I tried to improvise. We'd sit on the gallery. Uh-huh. And I would sing the melody of my number. Uh-huh. And she'd make the other part. And we'd continue that until I'd memorize it. Then I'd get her to band. Well, she must have done a…

677.t: Playing with his brothers and his father's musical family
677.s: He and Harold played together, Merrill accompanied him in church, and his father's family, including uncle James Bartlett Brown of a touring quartet, was very musical.
677.q: He was a piano -- concert piano type. And in fact he used to accompany me whenever I wanted to play a solo in church or something like that.

17.t: His musical brothers, sister and singing father
17.s: Brothers Teddy, Jay (Ruben) and Herbert play piano or drums, his sister played church piano, and their father had them sing syllables at the piano.
17.q: Yes, Teddy and Jay, June, or Ruben. Teddy played with Roy Eldridge around Chicago for a while. Then Jay has played with oh, different groups around, this Miss Rhapsody in Newark, New Jersey.

378.t: Brothers' and sister's talents; mother and the Hammond organ
378.s: His second brother was a gifted violinist who gave it up for football, his sister graduated in music, and his mother could play Bach but not improvise.
378.q: Yeah, but my second brother was really the most -- probably the greatest talent, he was a great violinist. He had a lot of scholarships offered him and he won a lot of things, but --

169.t: Musical half-brothers, grandmother in Sapulpa, grandfather the interpreter
169.s: His half-brothers all played music. Raised by his grandmother in Sapulpa while his grandfather preached in Indian languages; he skipped home life for music and knew Frank Wess and the Royal brothers.
169.ch: Childhood and first music in Oklahoma
169.q: Anyway, I wanted to play music, because my brother... I had three half-brothers, all of them played music. One of them was Ben Johnson, he was a bass guitar and piano player. My older brother, Joe, was a pianist, and my younger brother, Cesar Johnson, was a guitarist. So they were all that I knew…

388.t: Half sister and Uncle Clifford, a Bower-trained drummer
388.s: Half sister Pauline; Leeman was named for his uncle Clifford Francis Leeman, a New England Conservatory drummer who played with the Boston Symphony and gave up music for insurance.
388.q: Her name was Pauline Francis. And I was named after my uncle, who was my father's brother, who was Clifford Francis Leeman. He had a very decisive background, too. He graduated from the New England Conservatory of Music in 1915, and I have the original Owen Bauer Book, a hard cover, which is a…

171.t: Musical Ramey side: grandfather's violin, father's banjo, brother's quartet
171.s: His grandfather Jack Ramey played violin and patted his foot, as Ramey does; his father played banjo and his brother sang in a famous quartet.
171.q: On the Glasgow side, and also on the Ramey side, too, except that, you know how it is when your father dies, your mother doesn't tell you too much about those over on your father's side. We got the remnants of it later on. But my grandfather, Jack Ramey, was a whiz on violin. And they said -- funny…
